 'Most people don't answer polls': Joe Rogan points out major problem with Trump polling
 American podcaster Joe Rogan has questioned the accuracy of political polling, claiming the methods for political data collection are inherently flawed.
 Jaimee Marshall Lifestyle Reporter 4 min read November 1, 2026 - 4:50PM Joe Rogan is taking shots at the validity of political polling ahead of the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
 The UFC announcer and host of the Joe Rogan Experience had on TRIGGERnometry hosts Francis Foster and Konstatin Kisin as guests of his podcast's most recent episode, #2574.
 They discussed, among other things, the value of religion as a "social technology," the questionable validity of political polls, and the spread of misinformation online.
 When Rogan looked up a question about how religiously affiliated Republicans and Democrats are, he took note of a section about the percentage of people who didn't respond to polls.
 Joe Rogan hosting his podcast the Joe Rogan Experience, where he questioned the validity of political polling ahead of the US midterm elections. Picture: PowerfulJRE via YouTube. Rogan called such people "the most intelligent people on Earth."
 Rogan continued, "That was my take on my polls, always. I was like, 'Here's the problem with polls: Most people don't answer polls."
 "If somebody calls you up and said, 'I'd like a few moments of your time to ask you a few questions,' f*** you! Anybody with a life, anybody that has a family and stuff to do, hobbies they enjoy, friends they want to hang out with, they don’t sit around answering some f***ing poll."
 "So you're literally getting the opinion of people so f***ing stupid, they answer polls."
 Konstantin Kisin of TRIGGERnometry on JRE. Picture: PowerfulJRE via YouTube. Francis Foster of TRIGGERnometry on JRE. Picture: PowerfulJRE via YouTube. Rogan's comments come just days ahead of the US midterm elections which will determine which party wins control of Congress.
 Currently, Republicans hold a majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
 If polling , which is often difficult to gauge, especially in low-turnout elections like the midterms, are correct, Republicans will at least lose their majority in the House.
 However, they could also flip the Senate.
 Besides Trumps' approval rating falling to a new low, midterm elections often work to the benefit of the party not in power, who are more motivated to show up to vote.
 The three also discussed bad faith actors on social media. 
 “You have to really do a lot of research now to even know the basic facts of anything," Kisin said.
 "So, if you see something on X or Facebook or whatever, I am hesitant to believe it now off the top, do you know what I mean?”
 Rogan affirmed Kisin's concerns: "100 per cent. I read stories all day that I know are fake immediately and is like ‘breaking’ and then you read the thing in all caps and you’re like, ‘oh, this is a fake story’ and there’s a lot of them. They’re all over the place.”
 Rogan mentioned hearing X was demonetising those sorts of posts to disincentivise the spread of misinformation, but cautioned, “If the goal is propaganda, then they don’t care about the money," citing concerns about foreign governments exerting influence on American politics.
 Rogan suggested, “Maybe when there’s a fact check, like a Grok fact check and it proves to be absolutely incorrect, maybe they should just take it down so that you don’t have to go into the thread."
 The podcaster has personally been targeted for "misinformation" by fact checkers during COVID.
 Kisin added that the problem is “amplified by bots or foreign actors” and proposed a digital border enforcement as a solution, explaining it would help to know who the people commenting on something are and where they’re from.
 “I think most people get their political opinions from other people, Kisin said, adding that the appearance of a consensus on an issue can function as an informal type of political influence.
 The process of conforming to socially acceptable behavior is a concept known as “ social proof .”
 When humans are faced with ambiguity, we assume the people around us know more about the situation than we do.
 While there can be real value in "the wisdom of the crowd," when it comes to online interactions, "popular opinions" might be less popular than we think.
 Social media can propagate something known as the " majority illusion ," an effect that leads people to overestimate the prevalence of a state (such as an opinion) and accelerate the spread of social contagions.
 This happens when a state that is globally rare is over-represented in the local networks of individuals, such as in algorithmic echo chambers. 
 Rogan also expressed concern about bad faith actors trying to stir up engagement online with ‘rage bait’ content that is intentionally designed to provoke outrage and drive clicks.
 Rogan and Foster both expressed worry that X’s monetisation model encourages unproductive discourse.
 “Some people on Twitter (now X) just exist for engagement. They’re not good faith actors. They’re just weird people that are probably on all sorts of weird drugs and they’re somewhere just f***ing tweeting up a storm," Rogan said
 Kisin praised Rogan for being one of the few podcasters who talks to people across the political spectrum.
 “I actually kind of marveled at how you were able to do it because when we started, we had a very hard time getting more of the left-leaning guests on," he said.
 He added that Rogan never seemed to have that problem despite being culturally branded as a right-wing figure in recent years, especially after his endorsement of Donald Trump in the 2024 election.
 The endorsement was credited by Trump’s team as a “ major win ” in the final hours of election night.
 The podcaster has been increasingly critical of the Trump administration, claiming supporters feel betrayed by the administration’s military action in Iran after promising no new wars.

 “I think the outrage stuff you’re talking about; it pushes people apart. We were really interested in, ‘how do you bring people together to have one conversation based on an agreed set of facts?’”
 Rogan added that he thinks it’s possible so long as you only engage with people who are honest, good-faith conversationalists.
